subject: political-science
readings: PG ch. 1 (The Globalization of International Relations) + ch. 2 (Realist Theories) — Goldstein & Pevehouse

cards.front: Define **international relations (IR)** and say *why the field needs theories at all*.
cards.back:
**IR = the relationships among the world's governments**, tangled up with other actors (UN, corporations, individuals), other relationships (economics, culture), and history/geography.

We need **theories** because **facts don't explain themselves** — a theory turns *"what happened"* into *"why."* It's a **pair of glasses**: realism and liberalism look at the *same* event and each highlights different causes. IR is a **subfield of political science**; its two halves are **international security** and **international political economy (IPE)**.
cards.hint: Facts don't explain themselves.

cards.front: Define the **collective-goods problem** — IR's core puzzle — and why it's *especially hard internationally*.
cards.back:
**Collective-goods problem** = how can a group serve its **collective interest** when each member is tempted to put its **own** interest first? Everyone benefits from a **collective good** (clean climate, a strong alliance) *whether or not they help pay* — so each is tempted to **free-ride**, and if too many do, the good collapses.

It's the **group-project problem** at world scale. Domestically a **government** forces contributions (taxes); internationally there's **no world government**, so the problem is especially hard.
cards.hint: The group-project problem — everyone wants the grade, nobody does the work.

cards.front: Match each **solution to the collective-goods problem** to its logic: (a) *someone's the boss — obey those above you*; (b) *I'll help if you help; I'll hit back if you cheat*; (c) *we're family, so I give without keeping score*.
cards.back:
(a) **Dominance** — a **power hierarchy** imposes order top-down (a "government without a government"). Upside: order & stability / Downside: oppression & resentment.
(b) **Reciprocity** — **tit-for-tat**. Robust & self-enforcing / but downward spirals.
(c) **Identity** — a shared sense of **"we."** Deep cooperation / but can demonise an out-group.

**Realism is built on the *dominance* principle.**
cards.hint: Boss · tit-for-tat · family.

cards.front: **Nuclear non-proliferation** is the textbook case that runs on *all three* collective-good solutions at once. Name each mechanism at work.
cards.back:
**Dominance** — the UNSC "big five" keep the bomb (a power hierarchy).
**Reciprocity** — the **NPT bargain**: you stay non-nuclear, we disarm.
**Identity** — **Sweden / Japan** chose *not* to build one (a sense of who "we" are).

The point: real cooperation usually blends dominance + reciprocity + identity, not just one.
cards.hint: UNSC · NPT · Sweden/Japan.

cards.front: Define **state** (the four ingredients) and separate it from **nation** and **country**.
cards.back:
**State** = *"an inhabited territory controlled by a government that exercises **sovereignty**"* = **territory + government + sovereignty** (answers to no higher authority) **+ recognition** by others.

**State ≠ nation** (a shared identity) **≠ country.** A **nation-state** is one where the population shares a national identity. The modern state system is only **~500 years old** (before: empires, city-states, fiefs).
cards.hint: Territory + government + sovereignty + recognition.

cards.front: Name the **non-state actor type**: (a) members are national governments; (b) members are individuals & groups; (c) members are firms across borders.
cards.back:
(a) **IGOs** (intergovernmental orgs) — UN, NATO, WTO, EU.
(b) **NGOs** (non-governmental orgs) — Amnesty, Red Cross, Greenpeace.
(c) **MNCs** (multinational corporations) — ExxonMobil, Toyota, Walmart.

*Others:* individuals, cities, networks (Bono, al-Qaeda, Iraqi Kurdistan). There are **>50,000 NGOs**, **~5,000 IGOs**, and **193 UN members** (2018).
cards.hint: Governments · people · firms.

cards.front: Distinguish **sovereignty** from **anarchy** — and stress the one thing anarchy is *not*.
cards.back:
**Sovereignty** = a state's right to do as it likes **inside** its own borders (the **norm of non-interference**).

**Anarchy** = its flip side: *"not chaos, but the lack of a central government that can enforce rules"* — **"no world police."** No one stands above states to force them to keep promises or protect them, so realists say each must **look after itself** and watch others' **capabilities, not intentions**.

*Anarchy ≠ chaos:* **territorial integrity** and **diplomatic norms** (an embassy = home soil) keep the system remarkably orderly.
cards.hint: Inside-right vs no-enforcer-above.

cards.front: Match the **level of analysis** to the cause: (a) a leader's psychology; (b) democracy vs dictatorship / public opinion; (c) the balance of power & alliances; (d) technology & the environment.
cards.back:
(a) **Individual** — particular people's choices/psychology (*the person*).
(b) **Domestic** — groups *inside* a state (*the country's insides*).
(c) **Interstate / systemic** — states interacting; the **distribution of power** (*states vs states*).
(d) **Global** — worldwide forces (*the whole planet*).

None is *the* correct level. Higher levels change **more slowly**. **Realism lives mostly at the interstate/systemic level.**
cards.hint: Person · country's insides · states vs states · whole planet.

cards.front: Define **realism** and list its **five core assumptions**.
cards.back:
**Realism** = *"a broad tradition that explains IR mainly in terms of **power**"* — a **family** of theories, not one.

**Assumptions:** ① **states** are the key actors; ② each is a **unitary** actor (one voice — domestic politics is a *black box*); ③ each is a **rational** actor (defines interests, picks the option that maximises them); ④ the system is **anarchic**; ⑤ **power politics** trumps morality, ideology and economics.
cards.hint: States · unitary · rational · anarchy · power > morals.

cards.front: A realist says a state's decision to go to war can be **rational**. How — without claiming war is *good*?
cards.back:
**Rational ≠ good or moral.** A rational choice is just the best **cost–benefit** bet given the incentives.

*If a state calculates that the expected costs of **not** fighting exceed those of fighting, **war can be rational**.* Morality doesn't enter the calculation. This is why realism isn't *"war is good"* — it's *"given anarchy, this is the logic states are trapped in."*
cards.hint: Cost–benefit, not ethics.

cards.front: Contrast **realism** with **idealism / liberalism** on human nature and the international system.
cards.back:
**Idealists** see human nature as basically **good** and the system as a **community** that can cooperate.

**Realists** see human nature as **selfish** and the system as **anarchy** — and accuse idealists of studying the world as it *ought* to be, not as it *is*.

The lineage of realism: **Thucydides** (*"the strong do what they can, the weak suffer what they must"*) · **Machiavelli** (expedient power) · **Hobbes** (the anarchic "state of nature") · **Morgenthau** (*national interest defined as power*).
cards.hint: Selfish/anarchy/'is' vs good/community/'ought'.

cards.front: ★ Run the **realist causal chain** — the spine of the lecture — link by link.
cards.back:
**① Anarchy** (no world sovereign) → a state **can't trust** others to keep promises →
**② Uncertainty** → if no one guarantees your survival you must →
**③ Self-help** (arm, ally) → which means constantly judging your →
**④ Relative power** (capabilities vs others') → and everyone doing this at once produces →
**⑤ Competition** (alliances, arms races, war).

*Self-help ≠ never cooperate* — states cooperate, but always with one eye on how the deal shifts the **balance**.
cards.hint: Anarchy → uncertainty → self-help → relative power → competition.

cards.front: **Under Trump's Greenland threats, Denmark boosted conscription and Nordic defence ties — even though both are NATO allies.** Which link of the realist chain does this illustrate?
cards.back:
**Anarchy → uncertainty.** A state **can't fully trust** another to keep its word — so even between allies, DK couldn't rely on US respect for its sovereignty.

The response is textbook **self-help**: arm (conscription) and ally (Nordic military ties). It shows the chain operating even *inside* an alliance.
cards.hint: The trust-can't-be-assumed link.

cards.front: Distinguish the two ways realists think about **power**: power as **influence** vs power as **capability** — and name the best single yardstick.
cards.back:
**Power as influence** = getting another to do what it *wouldn't otherwise* do — but **circular** (we rarely know the "otherwise").
**Power as capability** = the *resources* behind influence — easier to **measure**.

**Best single yardstick = total GDP** (bundles size + wealth + technology), though only a *rough* estimator. Power is **relational**: *how capable am I **relative to you**?* For realists it's mostly **material / hard power** (Lukes' **1st face**).
cards.hint: Getting-you-to-act vs resources-behind-it; measure by GDP.

cards.front: Power-as-capability is a **bundle of resources**, sorted by *time horizon* and *tangibility*. Give the four boxes with examples.
cards.back:
**Long-term** (*who **will** be powerful*):
· Tangible — **GDP · population · territory · geography · natural resources.**
· Intangible — **political culture · patriotism · education · science/tech base · credibility/reputation · soft power.**

**Short-term** (influence *now*):
· Tangible — **military forces** (the realist's #1) · **military-industrial capacity.**
· Intangible — **legitimacy & support · loyalty** of army/politicians.

**Fungibility** = how far one element **converts into** another; **money is most fungible.**
cards.hint: Long/short × material/non-material.

cards.front: **At Pearl Harbor (1941) Japan had the military edge and overran the Pacific — yet the US ultimately overwhelmed it.** What lesson about power does this teach?
cards.back:
**Long-term power beats short-term power.** Japan had the **short-term military** edge, but the US's greater **long-term** resources (economic potential) let it build up and **overwhelm** Japan.

Lesson: **capabilities aren't just what you have now, but what you can *generate*.** (This is why realists rate long-term tangibles like GDP so highly.)
cards.hint: Now vs what you can generate.

cards.front: ★ The exam favourite: distinguish **relative gains** from **absolute gains**, and say who asks which.
cards.back:
A **liberal** asks *"do I gain?"* — **absolute gains.**
A **realist** asks *"do I gain **more than my rival**?"* — **relative gains** — because today's cooperation can fund tomorrow's threat.

*Worked case:* a deal gives you **+10** but your rival **+20** — a realist may **refuse**, because the rival's larger gain shifts the future **balance of power**. Examples: US–USSR nuclear parity; US–China tech race.
cards.hint: Do I gain? vs Do I gain *more than you*?

cards.front: Explain the **security dilemma** — why arming to feel safer can leave everyone *less* safe.
cards.back:
**Security dilemma** = when a state **arms to feel safer**, it makes others feel **less** safe, so they arm too — and everyone ends up **less secure**.

*In plain terms:* you buy a gun for self-defence; your neighbour feels threatened, buys two; now you're both more armed and **no safer**. It's a direct product of **anarchy** and the engine of **arms races**. Realists think it's **unsolvable** under anarchy; liberals think institutions can ease it.
cards.hint: Your defence looks like my threat.

cards.front: Define **balance of power**, and distinguish **internal** from **external balancing** (plus the "balancer").
cards.back:
**Balance of power** = a distribution in which **no single state can dominate** — because when power concentrates, others have an incentive to **counter** it. Can be an **outcome**, a **process** (balancing), or a **strategy**.

**Internal balancing** = build up *your own* capabilities.
**External balancing** = form **alliances**.
A **balancer** throws its weight against whoever is strongest (Britain in Europe for centuries).
cards.hint: Arm yourself vs make friends.

cards.front: Contrast **balancing** with **bandwagoning** — and add the twist about what states actually balance.
cards.back:
**Balancing** = counter the **strongest** state.
**Bandwagoning** = instead **jump on the bandwagon** of the winner (after WWII most states **joined** the US bloc rather than balancing it — a puzzle for pure balance-of-power theory).

**Twist:** states often balance **threats, not raw power** — US power was *greater* but *less threatening* than the USSR's, so allies balanced the Soviets.
cards.hint: Oppose the strong vs join the winner.

cards.front: Compare the three **polarity** types (multipolar / bipolar / unipolar) on hierarchy and stability — and state the book's counterintuitive finding.
cards.back:
**Multipolar** (5–6 powers) — *flat* hierarchy of shifting alliances; classic balance of power, but **war-prone**.
**Bipolar** (two blocs, e.g. Cold War) — dominance *within* blocs, reciprocity *between*; often judged **stable**.
**Unipolar / hegemony** (one dominant state) — the *steepest* hierarchy.

**Finding:** peace is best preserved by **hegemony**, next by **bipolarity** — *not* by multipolar equality. **Peace by inequality.**
cards.hint: Flat & war-prone → split & stable → steep & most stable.

cards.front: *"The biggest wars come when a **rising** power threatens to overtake the top state."* Name this theory and its nickname, with the current example.
cards.back:
**Power-transition theory** — nickname the **"Thucydides Trap."**

The most dangerous moment isn't equality but a **rising challenger** closing on the leader. Current example: **US–China.** (Links to relative gains and the whole polarity debate.)
cards.hint: Rising power vs top dog; a Greek historian's name.

cards.front: Define **hegemony** and **hegemonic stability theory** — including *why* the strongest would supply order for everyone.
cards.back:
**Hegemon** = a state with such a **preponderance of power** it can **single-handedly set the rules** of the system (Britain in the 1800s; the US after 1945).

**Hegemonic stability theory:** the system is most orderly when power is most **concentrated** — the hegemon supplies order like a stand-in government (deters aggression, underwrites free trade, provides a reserve currency).

*Why bother?* As the **biggest trader/producer** it **gains most** from an open, stable system it dominates. *Downside:* weaker states see it as **infringing sovereignty** (China uses "hegemony" as an insult).
cards.hint: One power sets the rules — and profits most from the order.

cards.front: Match the **realism variant** to its source of the power-drive: (a) human nature; (b) the anarchic structure itself; (c) structure + domestic factors as an intervening variable.
cards.back:
(a) **Classical realism** — **Morgenthau (1948)**: human nature + ambition, a timeless "struggle for power."
(b) **Structural / neorealism** — **Waltz (1979)**: the **anarchic structure** forces self-help, *not* human nature.
(c) **Neoclassical** — **Zakaria, Rose (1998)**: structure **+ domestic factors** (leaders, perceptions, state–society) as an **intervening variable**.

*In plain terms:* classical = *"it's our nature"*; structural = *"it's the situation"*; neoclassical = *"structure pushes, domestic politics filters the push."*
cards.hint: Nature · anarchy · anarchy-plus-domestics.

cards.front: ★ Compare **offensive** vs **defensive** realism (both structural) — the split that defines the whole family.
cards.back:
**Defensive realism** — **Waltz**: states are **security maximisers**, seeking *enough* power to be **safe**. Grabbing *too much* backfires — it triggers **balancing** and feeds the **security dilemma** — so a **balance of power** forms.

**Offensive realism** — **Mearsheimer (2001)**: states are **power maximisers**; *more* is always safer, so they seek to **dominate** and never settle for the BoP.

The core question: **is more power always safer, or does over-reach make you less safe?**
cards.hint: Enough to be safe vs the only safe amount is *all* of it.

cards.front: Run **offensive realism's** logic — *"the best defence is offence"* (Mearsheimer) — from anarchy to pre-emption.
cards.back:
**① Anarchy** → you can never be **sure** of another's **intentions** (they hide, and they change overnight) → so judge others by their **capabilities** (*"watch capabilities, not intentions"*).
**②** *Any* state with the **capability** to hurt you is a **potential** threat.
**③** So the *only* way to be **certain** you're safe is to be **more powerful than everyone else.**

Hence states are **power maximisers** who **expand — and will strike first (pre-emption)** — not out of greed but as the *safest* route to survival.
cards.hint: Can't read intentions → judge capability → out-power everyone → strike first.

cards.front: Define **alliance** the realist way — and use **NATO** to show alliances as *marriages of convenience*.
cards.back:
**Alliance** = a coalition of states coordinating (usually by treaty) against a **common threat.** Realists stress **fluidity** — alliances are *"marriages of convenience, not love,"* made and broken on **national interest** (*Palmerston: "no eternal allies… only perpetual interests"*). No element of power shifts as **fast** as an alliance.

**NATO** (1949) = US-led, built to **deter the USSR** (rival: the **Warsaw Pact**). **Article V** was first invoked *after 9/11* — **Europe defending the US**, the reverse of its original design. **Burden-sharing** (who pays) is the recurring intra-alliance fight.
cards.hint: Marriages of convenience; Article V invoked once, after 9/11.

cards.front: **NATO expanding east in waves (1999, 2004, …) toward Russia's borders.** Which realist mechanism reads this best, and how do the two sides see it?
cards.back:
Classic **security dilemma** material. The **West** sees expansion as **securing democracies** (a defensive move); **Russia** sees **encroachment** on its borders (a threat).

Each side's *"defensive"* move looks **threatening** to the other — the dilemma in action, with no enforcer above to reassure either. (This is the go-to case for the security dilemma.)
cards.hint: Securing democracies vs encroachment — the same move, two readings.

cards.front: Work the **Prisoner's Dilemma** (India–Pakistan nuclear, payoffs C/C=3,3 · defect dominates) — why do rational states end up *worse off*?
cards.back:
Cell = *(India, Pakistan)*, **4 = best, 1 = worst.** "Cooperate" = *don't* build the bomb; "Defect" = build it.

India's logic: *if Pakistan builds (right column), 2 > 1 → build; if Pakistan doesn't (left column), 4 > 3 → still build.* **Defecting dominates** → both build **(2, 2)**, even though **mutual cooperation (3, 3) is better for both.**

The tragedy: **individually rational → collectively worse.** (India tested 1998; Pakistan followed within weeks.) Realism's pessimism in a 2×2 box.
cards.hint: Defect dominates → both worse than (3,3).

cards.front: Distinguish **deterrence** from **compellence** — the strategies states use around the PD.
cards.back:
**Deterrence** = a threat to make an adversary **not act** (threaten punishment so an attack **never happens**).
**Compellence** = a threat to **force** an adversary to **act** (do something it otherwise wouldn't).

Both are tools to **escape or manage** the Prisoner's Dilemma and arms races — stopping an action vs forcing one.
cards.hint: Stop you acting vs make you act.

cards.front: ★ Big picture: everything in realism hangs on **one word — anarchy**. Trace how it drives trust, power, and even cooperation, and give the realist vs liberal split on the cooperation puzzle.
cards.back:
**Anarchy** (*not chaos — "no world police"*) → trust becomes **risky** → survival **can't be outsourced** → **power** (esp. material/military) is the currency → and because one state's gain can shift the **balance**, even **cooperation** is judged by **relative** advantage.

**The cooperation puzzle:** if the system is anarchic, why is cooperation sometimes deep (EU, WTO, NATO)?
**Realist answer:** institutions just **reflect the interests and power of the strongest states.**
**Liberal answer** (next lecture): institutions can **change the incentives** and make cooperation easier.
cards.hint: Ask of any event: how does 'no enforcer above states' drive it?
